transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-12-08
Start time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~58 minutes
Location: Zoom
Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Priya Natarajan (Redwood SE), Evan Torres (Redwood Solutions), Michael Chen (Everspring CTO), Sara Gomez (Everspring Lead Platform Engineer), Raj Patel (Security Architect), Aisha Khan (ML Engineer)

Summary (auto): Quick sync to map integration touchpoints. Customer has bursty QPS during market opens, strict encryption/KMS, and SSO requirement. Exploring hosted vs dedicated vs private; leaning private if latency and data residency can be guaranteed.

Transcript:
[00:00] Jordan Lee: hey everyone thanks for joining, i'm jordan, i'll kick us off. quick roll call?
[00:07] Michael Chen: michael here, sara, raj and aisha on our side.
[00:11] Sara Gomez: morning, doing great.
[00:13] Jordan Lee: perfect. priya from redwood?
[00:15] Priya Natarajan: hi all, priya se on infra, i'll steer the technical bits.
[00:20] Jordan Lee: goal for today is pretty pragmatic — figure out how everspring would integrate with redwood: sdk choices, gateway or proxy pattern, quotas and observability, and if private deployment is required what that looks like.
[00:33] Michael Chen: yep, high level — we run an insights platform for trading customers, traffic spikes a couple times a day, mostly short prompts but some long context sessions. security is key: SOC2, iso incoming, and KMS/HSM for key control.
[00:48] Priya Natarajan: makes sense. can you give a rough qps and average/95th latency target?
[00:55] Aisha Khan: baseline 50 rps avg, bursts up to 500 rps for 30-60s windows; target p95 latency under 250ms for short completions, for long context it's okay if it's 500-800ms.
[01:12] Raj Patel: and we need audit logs, token-level billing visibility is helpful for chargebacks, plus SSO with okta and idp rules.
[01:22] Jordan Lee: got it. so there are a couple of integration patterns we've seen work well: lightweight sidecar per service, a central gateway/proxy that routes to redwood, or direct SDK calls from the app. each has pros/cons for latency, observability, and quota enforcement.
[01:40] Michael Chen: what's the tradeoff between sidecar and central gateway? we've got a kubernetes microservices fleet.
[01:46] Priya Natarajan: sidecar is lower intra-cluster latency and easier local caching of prefixes / KV cache — but you have more instances to manage and consistent config push. central gateway simplifies quotas and global rate limiting and can provide a single observability sink; it may add a hop so add ~10-30ms typical. for everspring's burst pattern i'd lean central gateway with intelligent local caching at the sidecar or service level for hot keys.
[02:12] Sara Gomez: hot keys meaning repeated prompts? like templated queries?
[02:16] Priya Natarajan: yeah exactly. prefix caching and kv cache reuse. also we have automatic batching at the runtime layer if you funnel through a gateway. batching reduces cost but you need to consider latency SLOs.
[02:29] Michael Chen: and how do sdk integrations look — langchain and llamaindex? our pipelines use lang chain wrappers and some lama index connectors for retrieval.
[02:39] Priya Natarajan: we have first-class SDKs with adapters for LangChain and a LlamaIndex connector. note: sometimes transcription or naming changes in docs — people call it Lang Chain or Lama index — but the code paths are supported. the SDK exposes a retriever interface so you can swap in the redwood client for generation and embeddings.
[03:00] Aisha Khan: what's the easiest path for us to switch? minimal code changes?
[03:03] Priya Natarajan: typically you replace the llm client config and point the retriever to redwood embeddings endpoint. for llamaindex there's a one-line connector. for langchain you plug in the oak? — sorry, bad word — plug in the Redwood LLM wrapper; we can share a quick migration snippet.
[03:25] Jordan Lee: we'll attach sample snippets in the follow-up pack.
[03:29] Michael Chen: observability — we need tracing and token-level cost. how granular is the telemetry and what hooks do we have?
[03:37] Priya Natarajan: we expose request/response ids, per-request latency, token counts, and model variant info. we also support opentracing headers and you can forward traces to datadog or prom. plus event hooks for pre/post generation to capture prompts in your private deployment if you choose to. note on privacy we don't log prompt content on hosted unless allowed — but with private you control that.
[04:00] Raj Patel: okay good. and kms integration — do you support customer-managed keys?
[04:04] Priya Natarajan: yes, in private mode you can bring your own KMS/HSM and we integrate via key wrapping. for dedicated we support customer keys in some setups. we'll share more details in the security doc.
[04:18] Sara Gomez: rate limits/quota enforcement — we need per-tenant quotas for our customers plus global budget control. can redwood handle hierarchical quotas?
[04:27] Jordan Lee: yes we support nested quotas — account-level, tenant-level, and route-level. you can configure burst windows and soft/hard limits. on exceeding we return standard 429s and optional callback webhooks for consumed overage events.
[04:44] Aisha Khan: curious about throttling — we don't want request loss during bursts, can we queue?
[04:49] Priya Natarajan: there's request queuing in the gateway with backpressure signals to clients; also we recommend client-side retries with jitter. for mission-critical flows you can pair dedicated capacity with burst credits so you don't get throttled.
[05:02] Michael Chen: dedicated vs hosted vs private — cost differences?
[05:05] Jordan Lee: hosted is simplest and pay-as-you-go; dedicated reserves GPU pools for you for predictable perf and isolation; private gives you control over networking and keys (and is more similar to an on-prem license). pricing will vary — we'll share a sizing and pricing estimate after we see your workload sample.
[05:20] Sara Gomez: network: for private we need VPC peering and route tables, no public egress. is that supported?
[05:26] Priya Natarajan: yes, VPC peering or private link depending on cloud. we can do air-gapped on-prem as well but that adds lead time for packaging.
[05:35] Michael Chen: testing and benchmarks — what's typical for a POC?
[05:38] Priya Natarajan: we normally do a 2-week POC with a small set of endpoints: ingest sample traffic, run 95th latency and cost measurements, and test failure scenarios. we'll provide a benchmark harness (simple curl/golang or k6 script).
[05:52] Jordan Lee: okay action items: we'll send security pack, pricing, and a sample POC plan. can we aim to start the POC mid-december?
[05:59] Michael Chen: yes if we can get the papers and checklist early next week.
[06:03] Sara Gomez: one more — do you support per-route model pinning for rollouts? we want to canary a new model that reduces hallucinations but might be slightly slower.
[06:12] Priya Natarajan: yes we support per-route model pinning and rollout policies including canary, A/B and automatic fallback to a cheaper variant. you can also set quality gates based on eval datasets; if a metric regresses we can automatically route back.
[06:29] Raj Patel: audit logs retention and export — can we push them to our s3 or SIEM?
[06:34] Priya Natarajan: yes, export to s3 or forward to your SIEM, and retention policies are configurable in private/dedicated. hosted has default retention windows but enterprise add-ons extend that.
[06:48] Michael Chen: ok this is helpful. the main blockers are security and exact cost numbers. once we have those we'll pick between dedicated and private.
[06:57] Jordan Lee: fair. we'll follow up with the docs and pricing. next call, priya can do a 90-minute deep dive to walk through gateway code paths and run a quick profiler on a small sample.
[07:08] Aisha Khan: sounds good. thanks everyone.
[07:11] Jordan Lee: thanks all, we'll send notes and the pack today. bye.
[07:15] (call ends)
